title: GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs - deep dive (Valence AI)
header: Date: 2026-10-07 14:30 UTC | Duration: 78 min | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE), Marta Lopez (Valence Head of ML), Samir Gupta (Platform Eng), Emily Park (Infra), Jonas Berg (AI Research)
summary: Deep technical profiling session focused on kernel selection and runtime tradeoffs for Valence AI's 34B and 70B models. Compared TensorRT-LLM and vLLM behaviors, discussed CUDA graph stability, KV cache strategies, batching heuristics, and quantization impacts. Agreed on next steps: run end-to-end benchmark on Valence staging, collect kernel traces, and test fallback policies in VPC environment.
action_items: Jordan Patel - share initial kernel-level nvprof/NSight traces and a short how-to for reading them - due 2026-10-10
Marta Lopez - provide sample workload (prompt set + p99 latency SLO) and access to small staging dataset - due 2026-10-12
Riley Gomez - provision a 2xA100 test pool in Valence VPC for TensorRT experiments (with subnets) - due 2026-10-14
Samir Gupta - run baseline vLLM run and upload logs to shared bucket - due 2026-10-13
next_steps: Redwood to perform TensorRT-LLM quantized run + CUDA graphs and compare against vLLM baseline
Customer to share prompt set and staging cluster access
Schedule follow-up benchmark review next week (30-45m)
Exchange security docs for VPC/on-prem connectivity checklist
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll use this time to get into kernel selection and profiling for the 34B/70B stacks you mentioned. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Marta Lopez (Valence): Hey, Marta here — thanks. We have Samir, Emily and Jonas as well.
[00:12] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Jordan here, I'll drive the demos and traces later. Riley from infra is on too.
[00:18] Samir Gupta (Valence): Samir — we really want to understand why our p95 shot up last week after we moved to larger batch sizes.
[00:24] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): Quick note, there may be a little background noise from my side while I pull up traces.
[00:30] Jonas Berg (Valence): curious about quantization too — we saw accuracy drift with int8 on 70B in some setups.
[00:36] Alex Chen (Redwood): Great. Agenda: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA Graphs stability, KV cache eviction behavior, batching/cold-start latency, quantization regression patterns, and VPC/on-prem considerations.
[00:52] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): I'll start with kernel selection. Quick primer — our runtime picks kernels based on tensor shapes, sequence length, and the attention pattern. For some ops we prefer fused attention kernels (cuBLAS/cuDNN fused) and for others a custom CUDA kernel gives better memory locality.
[01:12] Marta Lopez (Valence): can you clarify "fused" vs "custom" here? sometimes our ops fallback to a generic kernel and that’s when we see spikes.
[01:20] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Yes, fused kernels are vendor-optimized combos — they reduce launches but require contiguous layout. Custom kernels we ship for KV-copy and rotary embedding are tuned for large sequence len. Fallbacks happen when shapes don't match the fast-path or when quantization forces an alternate layout.
[01:38] Samir Gupta (Valence): last week our seq len was variable, 32 to 1024, maybe that's the diff.
[01:44] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): variable seq is the classic pain. CUDA graphs help for stable sequences but tricky for mixed lengths.
[01:52] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Showed a trace: "nvprof/NSight timeline" image referenced (sent in chat).
[01:58] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): On the trace you can see repeated small kernel launches during KV updates causing CPU-GPU sync points. If you use CUDA Graphs to capture the recurrent execution, you collapse launches which reduces kernel launch overhead and dramatically lowers tail latency.
[02:18] Emily Park (Valence): we tried cudagraphs for encoder-decoder but got rare hangs under A100 drivers. Any known gotchas?
[02:26] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): driver hangs are usually from mutable memory captures — you must be careful to only capture immutable pointers, or regraph when shapes change. Also mixing cudagraphs with dynamic padding can break capture.
[02:40] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Another point — TensorRT-LLM uses more aggressive fusion and layerwise autotuning. In our tests, for 34B float16 it reduced avg latency by ~18% vs vLLM baseline, but for 70B the perf delta depends on batch shapes and KV access pattern.
[02:58] Marta Lopez (Valence): did you quantify p99 as well? our SLO is p99 <= 250ms for single-turn inference.
[03:06] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): In the lab, TRT-LLM + CUDA graphs delivered p99 improvements for stable seqs. But p99 sometimes regresses when we enable int8 quantization due to extra dequant/pack steps. So it's a tradeoff.
[03:18] Jonas Berg (Valence): about kv cache — we saw memory blowout when we pinned multiple concurrent sessions; what's Redwood's recommendation for eviction policies?
[03:28] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): We commonly use adaptive per-session KV caps and TTL-based eviction; for heavy multi-tenant loads we also store cold prefixes on host memory with a fast async fetch so GPU isn't overloaded.
[03:40] Samir Gupta (Valence): would that add additional latency?
[03:44] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Slightly for cold fetches, but you can mask with async prefetch and batching. In practice it reduces OOMs that cause big latency spikes.
[03:54] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Back to TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM — vLLM's continuous batching is excellent for throughput and mixed-length seqs, since it schedules micro-batches dynamically, but it has more kernel launch overhead. TRT-LLM trades launch count for heavier fused kernels. For latency-sensitive single-turn workloads TRT often wins if you can stabilize shapes.
[04:18] Emily Park (Valence): what about quantization artifacts — Jonas mentioned accuracy drift on int8 for our 70B. Any mitigations?
[04:26] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): We recommend per-layer calibration and selective quantization — keep MLP/attention in fp16 if you see drift, quantize feedforward layers. Also use PTQ with representative prompts instead of generic datasets.
[04:40] Marta Lopez (Valence): driver versions? we saw different behaviors between 545.x and 550.x.
[04:46] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): GPU driver and CUDA runtime mismatch frequently cause subtle perf cliffs. Always match vendor recommended stack for TensorRT. We maintain validated combos in our onboarding doc — we'll share the link.
[04:58] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Walkthrough of a typical profiling checklist: 1) run vLLM baseline with distributed profiler (we use py-spy/nsight), 2) collect kernel durations and memory ops, 3) run TRT-LLM conversion with sample inputs and validate logits, 4) test with CUDA graphs capture for stable sequence, 5) run mixed length stress tests.
[05:22] Samir Gupta (Valence): can Redwood help with the TRT conversion? our infra team hasn't done many manual kernel tuning steps.
[05:28] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Yes, we'll assist — Jordan will share step-by-step and kernels to watch. We can also run a pilot on your VPC if you give staging access.
[05:36] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Quick demo — posted a short GIF of timeline. You can see before/after: many small kernels turned into fused sequences.
[05:48] Jonas Berg (Valence): does that affect KV copy patterns? we rely on per-token KV updates for long contexts.
[05:54] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): For KV heavy workloads, we keep KV ops in a separate stream and use page-locked host buffers for staging. Fused kernels can reduce the number of syncs but you still need efficient memcpy patterns.
[06:06] Marta Lopez (Valence): Any advice for autoscaling and warm pools? we saw cold-start latency > 1s when scaling up GPUs.
[06:12] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): Warm pools are essential — pre-warmed models with cached KV and warmed cudagraphs reduce cold starts massively. Also keep minimal service on tail to avoid full cold boot.
[06:24] Emily Park (Valence): can we run Redwood's recommended bench script against our staging?
[06:28] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Yes — we'll provide the bench harness and a runbook. Expect to get a run in under an hour once staging cluster is ready.
[06:36] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Small note on CUDA graphs: when you capture, ensure that random seeds and dropout are disabled or fixed, otherwise captured ops may not reflect online behavior.
[06:50] Samir Gupta (Valence): about VPC & on-prem — we want to keep control plane on our side. Any blockers?
[06:56] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): We support Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane. Main considerations: KMS/HSM for keys, SAML/SSO for RBAC, and network egress rules for metrics. We also sign an SLA for Dedicated capacity.
[07:10] Marta Lopez (Valence): security will need SOC2 docs and audit logs for model access.
[07:14] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): We'll share SOC2 report and our audit log schema.
[07:18] Jonas Berg (Valence): curious about perf regressions after quantization — is there a deterministic checklist to validate quality?
[07:24] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Yes: 1) collect representative prompt set, 2) run baseline logits and top-k comparison, 3) compute perplexity and task metrics, 4) if delta > threshold, selectively revert layers or use mixed-precision. We'll share scripts.
[07:40] Emily Park (Valence): if we do int8, will we need to retrain?
[07:44] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Usually no retrain, PTQ is enough. Occasionally QAT is needed for edge cases but that's heavier.
[07:50] Samir Gupta (Valence): curious about cost delta — quantized TRT reduces GPU-hours, but conversion engineering costs more. any numbers?
[07:58] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): ballpark: 20-40% GPU-hour savings on steady-state throughput for int8/TensorRT on compatible models, but you'll spend 1-2 engineer-weeks in tuning per model family. We'll provide a cost model template.
[08:12] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): I'm going to demo two short logs: vLLM baseline vs TRT-LLM with cudagraphs.
[08:18] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): (shares console) On the vLLM run you see many kernel launches and an average kernel time of ~0.6ms for attention micro-ops; with TRT fused it's ~0.4ms but memory copy and dequant overhead appears in certain batches.
[08:36] Marta Lopez (Valence): what's the failover strategy if TRT fails in production?
[08:40] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): We recommend a canary with automatic fallback to vLLM variant. Our routing supports per-request policy: if TRT variant throws an error or exceeds latency threshold, route to fp16 vLLM. This keeps availability while you iterate.
[08:56] Jonas Berg (Valence): latency cost trade: if we pick TRT for single-turn latency, do we lose throughput at high concurrency?
[09:02] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): Not necessarily. If you stabilize shapes TRT scales well, but if you have many tiny concurrent sessions vLLM's dynamic batching can yield higher aggregated throughput. It's workload-dependent.
[09:18] Emily Park (Valence): can Redwood run a small A/B on our staging to measure both?
[09:22] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Yes — that's exactly the pilot we suggested. We'll run TRT vs vLLM on identical traffic and report cost/latency/quality.
[09:30] Samir Gupta (Valence): timeline? we'd like results before our next sprint planning.
[09:34] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): If you provide staging access and prompt set by Monday, Redwood can run the pilot by Thursday and present results Friday.
[09:42] Jordan Patel (Redwood SE): I'll drop the profiling runbook and a sample NSight capture command in Slack and the shared bucket. Also attaching a short README about CUDA graphs gotchas.
[09:54] Marta Lopez (Valence): thanks, that helps.
[09:58] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Quick recap: Redwood to share kernel traces, bench harness, and CUDA graphs notes. Valence to provide prompt set, staging access, and run vLLM baseline logs. Follow-up meeting next Friday to review benchmarks.
[10:14] Samir Gupta (Valence): one last question — any known incompatibilities with our on-prem racks (we run 2nd gen A100 equivalent)?
[10:20] Riley Gomez (Redwood SRE): Should be fine; main ask is driver/runtime alignment and enough pinned host memory for KV staging. We'll provide a preflight checklist.
[10:30] Jonas Berg (Valence): thanks all.
[10:34] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Thanks — we'll send notes and action items.
[10:38] (recording ended)
